entities.name: Hilary of Arles
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Hilary of Arles (c. 401–449 CE), also known by his Latin name Hilarius, served as the Metropolitan Bishop of Arles in Southern Gaul from 429 until his death. His episcopacy unfolded during a tumultuous period for the Western Roman Empire, marked by significant barbarian incursions and the ongoing theological disputes concerning grace and free will. As a prominent figure within the Gallic church, Hilary championed a vigorous monastic asceticism and asserted the primatial authority of the See of Arles over other bishops in Gaul, drawing the ire of Pope Leo I and Emperor Valentinian III. His life and controversies illuminate the complex interplay between spiritual authority, imperial power, and nascent regional ecclesiastical structures in the fading Roman West.

Born into an aristocratic aristocratic family in Gaul, Hilary initially pursued a secular career before embracing a monastic life under Honoratus, the founder of Lérins Abbey. Upon Honoratus's death in 429, Hilary was reluctantly consecrated as his successor to the See of Arles, a position he held for two decades. He was a prolific preacher and writer, though many of his works are lost, with his extant writings including a biography of Honoratus and several sermons. His most notable conflict arose from his efforts to enforce metropolitan authority, particularly his deposition of the bishop Projectus of Déas and his excommunication of Chelidonius of Besançon for alleged canonical irregularities, actions that directly challenged papal jurisdiction.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Hilary of Arles's conflict with Pope Leo I over metropolitan jurisdiction in Gaul led directly to an imperial decree that significantly bolstered the legal and political authority of the Roman See over regional churches, marking a pivotal step in the consolidation of papal power. His life exemplifies the complex interplay between local ecclesiastical autonomy and centralizing religious authority in the Late Roman West.
